problem: The shapes given are wrong for the loading stated. With width held constant, Z = bd²/6 ∝ d², so depth must vary as √M. For a cantilever with an end point load M ∝ x, giving d ∝ √x — a parabola in side view, not a triangle. The triangular side view (d ∝ x) belongs to a cantilever under a UDL, where M ∝ x². The simply supported UDL case is only parabolic if the depth is held constant and the width follows M.
fix: A cantilever under a UDL, constant width, has depth growing linearly from the free end — a triangle in side view. A cantilever with an end point load at constant width has depth growing as √x — a parabola in side view; if the depth is held constant instead, the width grows linearly and the beam is a triangle in plan. A simply supported beam under a UDL is parabolic in plan when the depth is kept constant.

problem: "No amount of extra depth will rescue it — you need area" is false. Adding depth increases the area A = bd in proportion, so it lowers τ_max = 1.5V/A exactly as widening does. A student will remember that depth is useless against shear, which is wrong.
fix: In a short span carrying a big load it decides the section. Shear is bought with area A = bd, from width or from depth; extra depth helps only in direct proportion to the area it adds, without the squared advantage it gives in bending.

problem: "Deepening alone barely helps because τ depends on area, not on d²" repeats the misconception of Section 2. It does help, linearly, because it adds area.
fix: Deepening helps only in proportion to the area it adds, since τ = 1.5V/(bd), while the same depth in bending raises Z with d². Widening helps shear and bending only linearly.

problem: "Every fibre is at the allowable stress" is not true. Only the extreme fibre of each cross-section reaches σ_allow; the stress falls to zero at the neutral axis.
fix: The extreme fibre is at the allowable stress at every section, so no material is carried where the moment cannot use it.
